content: Torque, in the field of physics, is a vector quantity that quantifies the tendency of a force to cause an object to rotate about a specific axis or pivot point. The magnitude of torque is calculated as the product of the applied force and the length of the lever arm (or radius) through which the force acts. Conceptually, torque can be thought of as a twisting force. Its standard unit in the International System of Units (SI) is the newton-meter (N·m), while in the customary system, it is measured in foot-pounds (ft·lbf). The symbol for torque is τ, derived from the Greek letter tau. The concept of torque, also referred to as moment or couple, has its origins in the studies of Archimedes on levers. In rotational dynamics, torque serves as the rotational analogue of force, while moment of inertia and angular acceleration correspond to mass and linear acceleration, respectively. The torque exerted by a force applied to a lever is determined by multiplying the force by its perpendicular distance from the fulcrum. For instance, a force of 3 newtons applied 2 meters from the fulcrum generates the same torque as a force of 1 newton applied 6 meters from the fulcrum, assuming the force acts at a right angle to the lever. The direction of the torque vector can be determined using the right-hand rule: curl the fingers of your right hand in the direction of rotation, and your thumb will point along the axis of rotation, indicating the direction of the torque vector. Mathematically, torque on a particle with position vector r in a reference frame is defined as the cross product of the position vector and the force vector. Torque determines the rate of change of angular momentum of a body. As a vector quantity, torque points along the axis of the rotation it tends to induce. Torque has the dimensions of force multiplied by distance, and its SI unit is the newton-meter (N·m). Although the joule (J) is also defined as 1 N·m, it is not used for torque because energy is a scalar quantity, while torque is a vector. The dimensional equivalence between these units is not coincidental; for example, a torque of 1 N·m applied through a full revolution requires an energy expenditure of exactly 2π joules. In extended SI systems, torque can also be expressed in terms of newton-meters per radian (N·m/rad) or joules per radian (J/rad) when considering rotational angles. This distinction is particularly useful when analyzing systems involving rotational motion, such as wheels in contact with surfaces. In such cases, the effective distance traveled by the center of the wheel may differ from the theoretical arc length due to energy losses from friction and sliding. These losses do not affect the measurement of torque but do influence the efficiency of the system. A special case of torque, often used in fields outside physics, involves the moment arm formula. This approach calculates the magnitude of torque as the product of the force and the perpendicular distance to the axis of rotation. However, this method does not provide the direction of the torque vector, making it less applicable in three-dimensional scenarios. When the force is perpendicular to the displacement vector, the moment arm equals the distance to the center, and the torque is maximized for a given force. If a force is applied at an angle θ to the displacement arm of length r, the magnitude of the resulting torque is given by the cross product definition, incorporating the sine of the angle between the force and the arm. For an object to achieve static equilibrium, both the sum of forces and the sum of torques about any point must equal zero. In two-dimensional systems, this condition is expressed through three equations: ΣH = 0, ΣV = 0, and Στ = 0. Torque is also the time derivative of angular momentum, analogous to how force is the time derivative of linear momentum. For a rigid body, angular momentum can be expressed in terms of its moment of inertia (I) and angular velocity (ω). If the moment of inertia is constant, torque is directly proportional to angular acceleration (α), which is typically measured in radians per second squared. In the context of engines, torque is a fundamental specification. The power output of an engine is the product of its torque and rotational speed. Internal combustion engines produce useful torque over a limited range of rotational speeds, typically between 1,000 and 6,000 rpm for small cars. The torque output across this range can be measured using a dynamometer and represented as a torque curve. The peak torque usually occurs below the peak power output. Understanding the relationship between torque, power, and engine speed is critical in automotive engineering, particularly for optimizing drivetrain gearing to match the engine's torque characteristics. Steam engines and electric motors, in contrast, tend to produce maximum torque at low rotational speeds, with torque diminishing as speed increases due to friction and other constraints. Consequently, these engines often require different drivetrain designs compared to internal combustion engines. Torque is also a straightforward way to explain mechanical advantage in simple machines. The relationship between torque, power, and energy is analogous to that between force, work, and energy in linear systems. When torque acts through a rotational distance, it performs work. Power is the rate of work done over time. The power injected by torque depends only on the instantaneous angular speed, not on whether the angular speed is increasing, decreasing, or constant. In practical applications, such as power stations connected to electrical grids, the generator's angular speed is fixed by the grid's frequency, and the power output is determined by the torque applied to the generator's axis. Consistent units must be used in calculations. In SI units, power is measured in watts, torque in newton-meters, and angular speed in radians per second. While the newton-meter is dimensionally equivalent to the joule, it is assigned to a vector for torque and a scalar for energy. For conversions between different units of power, torque, or angular speed, appropriate conversion factors must be applied. For example, if rotational speed is measured in revolutions per unit time instead of radians per unit time, a factor of 2π must be included to account for the 2π radians in a revolution. In the American system, power is often expressed in horsepower, torque in foot-pounds, and angular speed in revolutions per minute (rpm). For rotating objects, the linear distance covered at the circumference in one radian of rotation is the product of the radius and angular speed. Linear speed is thus the product of radius and angular speed. By definition, linear distance equals linear speed multiplied by time, which can also be expressed as radius times angular speed times time. Torque, defined as force times radius, can be rearranged to express force as torque divided by radius. Substituting these values into the definition of power yields a relationship where angular speed must be in radians for consistency. If rotational speed is measured in revolutions per unit time, linear speed and distance are proportionally increased by 2π, leading to a modified power equation.
